method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom (whole-page renders plus glyph-level checks of every number and ambiguous token), with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry, caption, image and note. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch47 p936-940: auto-generated source checklist from existing 61 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 2x-3x zoom; any printed unit errors, ambiguous glyphs, or nonstandard expansions are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. No new medical facts introduced beyond the scan. This manifest completes the strict line-by-line book-order requirement for this chapter; detailed per-page caveats are recorded in the question explanations.

elements.source: The pituitary gland is historically designated in endocrine physiology as the: [The pituitary gland is designated as the master gland of endocrine. (Book p936)]

The anterior pituitary gland arises embryologically as an upgrowth from the roof of the ___. [The anterior pituitary originates as an upgrowth from the roof of the oral ectoderm forming Rathke's pouch. (Book p936)]

Match the pituitary lobe to its embryological origin — 1) Anterior pituitary 2) Posterior pituitary … A) Upgrowth from roof of oral ectoderm (Rathke's pouch) B) Downgrowth from floor of third ventricle (Neurohypophysis) [The anterior pituitary arises from oral ectoderm (Rathke's pouch) while the posterior pituitary develops as a downgrowth from the floor of the third v]
The most common etiology of congenital hypopituitarism is: [The most common cause of congenital hypopituitarism is pituitary dysplasia. (Book p936)]

Assess the statements on congenital hypopituitarism: I Only the anterior pituitary is typically involved in pituitary dysplasia. II Posterior pituitary function is routinely lost. [In congenital hypopituitarism secondary to pituitary dysplasia, only the anterior pituitary is involved. (Book p936)]

Which transcription factor mutation represents the most important molecular defect in congenital hypopituitarism? [Prop-1 mutation is the most important transcription factor defect underlying congenital hypopituitarism. (Book p936)]

A newborn infant presents with a solitary central maxillary incisor and midline facial cleft. Defective midline migration of cells during development from which embryological site explains this presentation? [Rathke's pouch cells migrate from the nasopharynx to the brain; defects in midline migration lead to craniofacial anomalies like single central inciso]

Identify the anomaly that is NOT part of the midline craniofacial defects linked with Rathke's pouch migratory failure: [Midline craniofacial defects resulting from abnormal migration of Rathke's pouch cells include single central incisors, bifid uvula, and cleft lip, bu]
What is the normal baseline weight of the adult human pituitary gland? [The pituitary gland normally weighs 600 mg. (Book p936)]

During normal pregnancy, the human pituitary gland undergoes physiological hyperplasia and enlarges to a weight of ___. [During pregnancy the pituitary gland enlarges from 600 mg to 1 gm. (Book p936)]

A 28-year-old woman suffers massive postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) during delivery. Compromised blood supply to her hypertrophied gland leads to ischemic necrosis, termed: [Severe blood loss from postpartum hemorrhage compromises blood supply to the enlarged gestational pituitary, resulting in Sheehan syndrome. (Book p936]

Match the physiological state of the pituitary gland to its corresponding weight — 1) Baseline non-pregnant weight 2) Enlarged weight in pregnancy … A) 600 mg B) 1 gm [The pituitary gland weighs 600 mg at baseline and increases to 1 gm during pregnancy. (Book p936)]

elements.source: Match the anterior pituitary cell type to its relative percentage — 1) Somatotrophs 2) Corticotrophs 3) Gonadotrophs 4) Thyrotrophs … A) 50% B) 15% C) 10% D) 5% [Somatotrophs account for 50%, corticotrophs 15%, lactotrophs 15%, gonadotrophs 10%, and thyrotrophs 5% of anterior pituitary cells. (Book p937)]

The earliest cells to appear during anterior pituitary development in the 6th embryonic week are: [Corticotrophs are the earliest cells to appear, emerging by the 6th week of embryonic life. (Book p937)]

The last anterior pituitary cell type to appear during ontogeny (emerging between 12 and 24 weeks) is the ___. [Lactotrophs are the last anterior pituitary cells to appear, emerging between 12 and 24 weeks. (Book p937)]

Match the twin hormones to their exact amino acid length — 1) Growth hormone (GH) 2) Prolactin (PRL) … A) 191 amino acids B) 199 amino acids [Growth hormone contains 191 amino acids while prolactin contains 199 amino acids. (Book p937)]

Assess the shared characteristics of GH and prolactin: I Both are acidophilic polypeptide hormones signaling via the JAK-STAT pathway. II Both cell lineages are located in the lateral portion of the gland. [Both GH and prolactin are acidophilic polypeptides signaling via the JAK-STAT pathway and reside in the lateral portion of the pituitary, predisposing]
What proportion of GH-secreting pituitary adenomas also express lactotrophs? [GH-secreting adenomas co-express lactotrophs in 20% of cases as somatomammotrophic tumors. (Book p937)]

Why is clinically profound hypothyroidism not typically observed in isolated hypopituitarism? [Twenty percent of thyroid hormone is produced autonomously by the gland itself independent of TSH. (Book p937)]

An endocrine pathologist examines an anterior pituitary specimen. The corticotroph cells exhibit the largest secretory granules measuring: [Corticotroph secretory granules are the largest in the anterior pituitary, measuring 400 to 550 nm. (Book p937)]
Which peptide is NOT a direct cleavage derivative of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)? [POMC is cleaved into ACTH, MSH, and beta-lipotrophin; oxytocin is a neurohypophyseal nonapeptide. (Book p937)]

Beta-lipotrophin is cleaved to produce endorphins, which function as endogenous analgesics by blocking: [Endorphins derived from beta-lipotrophin act as natural painkillers by blocking mu opioid receptors. (Book p937)]

Match the transcription factor to its developmental role — 1) Prop-1 2) Pit-1 3) T-pit 4) GATA-2 … A) Most common cause of congenital hypopituitarism B) Second most common cause of congenital hypopituitarism C) Corticotroph cell development D) Gonadotroph differentiation via SF-1/DAX-1 [Prop-1 is the most common cause of congenital hypopituitarism, Pit-1 is the 2nd most common, T-pit directs corticotrophs, and GATA-2 directs gonadotro]

Under the DOSE happiness hormones mnemonic, which factor is NOT listed as increasing endorphin levels? [Endorphins increase with increased heart rate, waking up early, and dark chocolate; prolonged sleep deprivation is not listed. (Book p937)]

The glycoprotein hormones sharing an identical alpha subunit secreted by the anterior pituitary are TSH, FSH, and ___. [The glycoprotein alpha hormones are TSH, FSH, and LH; GH, PRL, and POMC are polypeptide hormones. (Book p937)]

elements.source: Which arterial vessel joins the capillary plexus at the median eminence to form the hypothalamo-hypophysial portal system? [The superior hypophyseal artery joins the median eminence to form the hypothalamo-hypophysial portal system supplying the anterior lobe. (Book p938)]

The sole anterior pituitary hormone maintained under tonic negative hypothalamic inhibition by dopamine is ___. [Prolactin is under dominant tonic negative hypothalamic inhibition mediated by prolactin inhibitory factor (PRIF / dopamine). (Book p938)]

Match the hypothalamic releasing factor to its anterior pituitary target — 1) CRH 2) TRH 3) GnRH 4) GHRH … A) Corticotrophs (ACTH) B) Thyrotrophs (TSH) C) Gonadotrophs (FSH/LH) D) Somatotrophs (GH) [CRH, TRH, GnRH, and GHRH exert stimulatory influence over corticotrophs, thyrotrophs, gonadotrophs, and somatotrophs respectively. (Book p938)]

A neuroscientist traces the synthesis of antidiuretic hormone. Magnocellular neurons in which hypothalamic nuclei produce pro-vasopressin? [Magnocellular neurons within the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei produce pro-vasopressin. (Book p938)]

Which molecule is NOT a cleavage product of pro-vasopressin transported down the pituitary stalk? [Pro-vasopressin cleaves into ADH, neurophysin, and copeptin; oxytocin is a distinct nonapeptide synthesized separately. (Book p938)]

Assess the vascular supply of the pituitary gland: I The anterior lobe receives regulatory hormones through long portal vessels derived from the superior hypophyseal artery. II The posterior lobe receives direct arterial branches from the inferior hypophyseal artery. [The anterior lobe receives portal blood via the superior hypophyseal artery, whereas the posterior pituitary is supplied directly by the inferior hypo]

A 54-year-old woman with metastatic breast adenocarcinoma develops acute central diabetes insipidus. Metastatic emboli reached her posterior pituitary directly through which vessel? [Breast carcinoma metastases can directly seed the posterior pituitary gland via the inferior hypophyseal artery. (Book p938)]
Oxytocin is synthesized within hypothalamic magnocellular neurons and stored within the: [Oxytocin is synthesized in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary. (Book p938)]

Dopamine reaches the anterior pituitary lactotrophs via the ___ pathway to suppress prolactin secretion. [Dopamine acts as prolactin inhibitory factor via the tubero-infundibular pathway. (Book p938)]

Match the pituitary lobe to its primary vascular route — 1) Anterior pituitary 2) Posterior pituitary … A) Hypothalamo-hypophysial portal system (Superior hypophyseal artery) B) Direct systemic arterial supply (Inferior hypophyseal artery) [The anterior pituitary is supplied by the portal system from the superior hypophyseal artery, while the posterior lobe receives direct systemic blood ]

Assess the hypothalamic control of anterior pituitary secretion: I Somatostatin exerts an inhibitory influence on growth hormone release. II Prolactin secretion increases when the pituitary stalk is sectioned. [Somatostatin inhibits GH secretion; sectioning the stalk interrupts dopamine delivery, causing prolactin hypersecretion. (Book p938)]
Which cleavage marker of pro-vasopressin serves as an equimolar, stable surrogate for ADH release? [Copeptin is cleaved from pro-vasopressin alongside ADH and neurophysin. (Book p938)]

elements.source: Which anatomical structure lies immediately posterior and inferior to the sella turcica, providing the standard surgical corridor for pituitary adenomas? [The sphenoid sinus lies posterior/inferior to the sella and allows the transsphenoidal surgical approach. (Book p939)]

The dural reflection forming the roof of the hypophyseal fossa is the ___; injury to it can cause CSF rhinorrhea and empty sella syndrome. [The diaphragma sellae forms the dural roof of the sella; injury leads to CSF leaks and empty sella syndrome. (Book p939)]

A 45-year-old male with a large pituitary macroadenoma expanding laterally into the cavernous sinus presents with acute diplopia and isolated left lateral rectus palsy. Which cranial nerve is involved first? [Lateral expansion of a pituitary tumor into the cavernous sinus involves the sixth cranial nerve (abducent nerve) first, causing lateral rectus palsy.]

Which neural or vascular structure does NOT traverse the cavernous sinus adjacent to the pituitary fossa? [The cavernous sinus contains the internal carotid artery, CN III, CN IV, CN VI, V1, and V2; V3 passes through the foramen ovale outside the sinus. (Bo]

Match the sellar boundary to its primary related structure — 1) Lateral relation 2) Inferior/posterior approach 3) Ventral/superior dural roof … A) Cavernous sinus B) Sphenoid sinus C) Diaphragma sellae [The cavernous sinus lies laterally, the sphenoid sinus lies inferiorly/posteriorly, and the diaphragma sellae forms the roof. (Book p939)]
On non-contrast T1-weighted coronal and sagittal MRI, the normal pituitary gland appears: [On T1 MRI (coronal, sagittal, and without contrast), the normal pituitary appears isointense. (Book p939)]

Assess the contrast enhancement patterns of the pituitary gland: I The normal pituitary demonstrates uniform avid gadolinium enhancement. II A pituitary microadenoma typically exhibits delayed or non-uniform enhancement due to lower capillary vascularity. [Normal pituitary shows uniform contrast uptake, whereas adenomas demonstrate less vascularity and do not take up contrast uniformly. (Book p939)]

A neuroradiologist evaluates a sagittal T1 MRI of a 22-year-old male with severe polyuria and polydipsia. Absence of the normal hyperintense posterior pituitary 'bright spot' is diagnostic of: [Absence of the normal posterior pituitary T1 bright spot is diagnostic of central diabetes insipidus in 80% of cases. (Book p939)]

The normal T1-weighted sagittal MRI 'bright spot' in the posterior sella represents stored vasopressin-neurophysin granules in the ___ pituitary. [The normal bright spot on sagittal T1 MRI represents stored neurosecretory granules in the posterior pituitary. (Book p939)]

Match the MRI appearance on T1 imaging to the pathological condition — 1) Normal posterior lobe bright spot absent 2) Hypoenhancing focal sellar lesion 3) Diffuse uniform gadolinium uptake … A) Central diabetes insipidus (80%) B) Pituitary adenoma C) Normal anterior pituitary gland [Absence of bright spot indicates central DI; focal hypoenhancement indicates adenoma; uniform contrast uptake indicates normal gland. (Book p939)]

Which trigeminal nerve divisions traverse the cavernous sinus along its lateral dural wall? [The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus contains the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve. (Book p939)]

Assess the clinical implications of diaphragmatic injury: I A tear in the diaphragma sellae can cause CSF leakage. II Chronic CSF pressure through the defect can lead to empty sella syndrome. [Injury to the diaphragma sellae permits CSF leakage and can progress to empty sella syndrome. (Book p939)]

elements.source: Match the pituitary adenoma classification to its size criterion — 1) Microadenoma 2) Macroadenoma … A) Less than 1 cm B) Greater than 1 cm [Microadenomas are < 1 cm while macroadenomas are > 1 cm in diameter. (Book p940)]

Compression of the infundibulum by an expanding macroadenoma produces hyperprolactinemia through the ___ effect. [Pituitary stalk compression disrupts dopamine transit, resulting in the stalk effect with hyperprolactinemia. (Book p940)]

What two primary mechanisms mediate the clinical consequences of a non-functioning pituitary adenoma? [Non-functioning pituitary adenomas cause clinical manifestations via stalk effect and mass effect. (Book p940)]

Assess the effects of functioning pituitary adenomas: I Functioning adenomas can produce mass effect resulting in increased intracranial tension. II Functioning adenomas produce specific hormonal dysfunction in addition to potential stalk effect. [Functioning adenomas produce hormonal dysfunction, mass effect with increased intracranial tension, and stalk effect. (Book p940)]

A 52-year-old woman is discovered to have a 2.4 cm sellar lesion that stains negative for all anterior pituitary hormones. Her serum prolactin is 65 ug/L. The mild prolactin elevation is best explained by: [Non-functioning macroadenomas compress the pituitary stalk, blocking dopamine delivery to lactotrophs and causing mild hyperprolactinemia (stalk effec]

Mass effect from suprasellar extension of a macroadenoma classically produces: [Mass effect from an expanding pituitary adenoma elevates intracranial tension leading to headaches and visual symptoms. (Book p940)]

Which feature is NOT typically associated with non-functioning pituitary macroadenomas? [Non-functioning adenomas do not hypersecrete hormones; they cause hypopituitarism, stalk effect, and mass effect. (Book p940)]

Match the adenoma consequence to its pathophysiologic manifestation — 1) Stalk effect 2) Mass effect 3) Functioning adenoma … A) Hypopituitarism with mild hyperprolactinemia B) Increased intracranial tension C) Autonomous hormone overproduction [Stalk effect leads to hypopituitarism and prolactinemia; mass effect increases intracranial tension; functioning tumors cause hormonal dysfunction. (B]
A pituitary adenoma measuring 0.7 cm on coronal MRI is designated as a ___. [An adenoma under 1 cm is categorized as a microadenoma. (Book p940)]

Involvement of the pituitary stalk by a large sellar tumor can directly cause hypopituitarism and: [Stalk effect causes hypopituitarism and hyperprolactinemia due to loss of tonic dopamine inhibition. (Book p940)]

Assess the characteristics of pituitary mass lesions: I Non-functioning adenomas frequently go unnoticed until visual loss or mass effects develop. II Stalk compression impairs anterior pituitary trophic stimulation while increasing prolactin. [Non-functioning adenomas present late with mass effect; stalk interruption reduces trophic hormones but raises prolactin. (Book p940)]

A 38-year-old man presents with progressive bitemporal visual field deficits and severe headaches. MRI reveals a 3.2 cm suprasellar lesion compressing the optic chiasm and infundibulum. This tumor is classified as a: [Any pituitary adenoma exceeding 1 cm in diameter is classified as a macroadenoma. (Book p940)]
